walkthroughs.body_html:
The Water Cycle & Water Insecurity — a core area of A-Level Geography.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

The Water Cycle & Water Insecurity brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with The Water Cycle & Water Insecurity.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Lag time on a storm hydrograph is the time between:
options: Peak rainfall and peak discharge
The start and end of the storm
Baseflow and stormflow
Two successive flood events

mcqs.q: Physical water scarcity differs from economic water scarcity because:
options: Supply itself is insufficient, rather than access and infrastructure being lacking
It only occurs in wealthy countries
It is caused by water being too expensive
It can be solved without any investment

mcqs.q: Which process moves water from vegetation into the atmosphere?
options: Transpiration
Infiltration
Percolation
Throughflow
Flashier — shorter lag time and higher peak — because impermeable surfaces speed up runoff
Flatter, with a longer lag time and lower peak
Completely unchanged
Impossible to measure

mcqs.q: Does groundwater refill as quickly as it is pumped out?
options: Water scarcity only happens in winter.
Groundwater is manufactured in water treatment plants.
Groundwater is effectively unlimited because rain constantly tops it up.
Usually not — aquifer recharge can take decades to millennia, so abstraction above the recharge rate effectively mines the store and water tables fall.

mcqs.q: Is water scarcity only caused by dry climates?
options: Only desert countries can suffer water insecurity.
Groundwater is manufactured in water treatment plants.
Water scarcity only happens in winter.
No — economic water scarcity occurs where rainfall is adequate but infrastructure and investment are lacking, as in much of sub-Saharan Africa.

mcqs.q: Do large dams solve water insecurity?
options: Only partially — reservoirs store and regulate supply, but they lose water to evaporation, trap sediment, displace communities and reduce flows downstream, sometimes shifting insecurity elsewhere.
Dams work by creating new rainfall.
Building a big dam permanently fixes a region's water problems.
Groundwater is manufactured in water treatment plants.
